OPS06-BP01 Create actionable alerts
When each alert maps to a defined response, operators know what to
    do when it fires, and important signals aren't lost in low-value
    noise.
Desired outcome:
Your alerts fire on conditions that represent problems, such as
        an objective at risk, not on every raw metric deviation.
Each of your alerts maps to a specific, documented response, and
        where possible you automate that response.
Each of your alerts has a clear owner and a defined escalation
        path, so no notification is left unattended.
Your alerts link to current runbooks or playbooks, so any
        operator can respond the same way.
Your alert volume stays low enough that operators treat each
        alert as meaningful rather than background noise.
Common anti-patterns:
Teams raise alerts that describe a symptom but carry no defined
        response, so operators improvise during incidents.
Monitoring generates so many low-value alerts that operators
        overlook the ones that matter.
Alerts have no assigned owner, so handling depends on whoever
        happens to notice.
Operators respond to the same alert differently each time
        because no shared response process exists.
Alerts fire on raw metrics without correlation, producing a
        burst of notifications for a single underlying problem.
Benefits of establishing this best
    practice:
Operators experience less alert fatigue because only actionable
        alerts reach them.
Mean time to resolution (MTTR) drops because each alert carries
        a known response.
Mean time to investigate (MTTI) drops, which further reduces
        MTTR.
Operational responses scale because responses are documented and
        often automated.
Incident handling stays consistent and reliable across teams and
        shifts.
Level of risk exposed if this best practice
    is not established:
High
Implementation guidance
An actionable alert tells an operator what is wrong and what to do
      about it. Monitoring can emit a signal for almost any state
      change, but few of those signals need human attention. If an alert
      fires, someone or something must act. Signals that carry no
      response belong on a dashboard or in a log. The alerting signal
      can be a metric, a service level objective, or a recurring log
      signal turned into a metric
      (
OPS02-BP04 Regularly analyze workload logs
).
Alert fatigue is the dominant failure mode, where operators
      receive hundreds of notifications a day and learn to ignore them.
      Then, the one alert that signals a real incident is lost with the
      rest. The usual cause is alerting on raw metrics. Instead, alert
      on conditions that represent actual problems. A single failing
      dependency can trip a dozen metric thresholds, producing many
      alerts for one root cause. Aggregating related signals into a
      composite condition reduces alert fatigue and produces one
      actionable alert.
Every threshold is a trade-off between sensitivity and precision.
      A tight threshold can miss early warnings of a developing problem,
      while a loose one can bury operators in false positives. Tune
      thresholds against historical data, and revisit them as the
      workload changes. An alert that is useful at launch can become
      useless a year later depending on changes to your workload. Some
      metrics have no fixed threshold, and their normal range might
      shift with time of day or day of week. Anomaly detection alarms
      learn each metric's normal band and fire on deviations.
For workloads instrumented with OpenTelemetry,
CloudWatch Omni alerts
add timing controls such as a pending duration,
      so a single spike does not send an alert, and a recovery duration,
      so a flapping signal does not resolve and fire again. One Omni
      alert also contains warning and critical tiers, each routable to a
      destination, so the same condition can warn a team channel before
      its critical tier reaches an on-call engineer. Omni alerts are
      separate from CloudWatch alarms, which continue to work unchanged.
Alert conditions form a hierarchy, and you should start at the
      top. Business outcome metrics, for example the KPIs from
OPS02-BP01 Develop key performance indicators
, and RED metrics (rate, errors,
      duration) are closest to what users experience. They move only
      when something important is at stake, so they produce the least
      noise. Where service-level objectives exist, alarm on the error
      budget burn rate, or how fast the service is consuming its
      allowance for failure. A fast burn demands interruption, and a
      slow burn can wait for review. The alert carries its own urgency,
      and its threshold reflects the objective (for more detail, see
OPS02-BP05 Regularly analyze workload traces
).
Work down the stack deliberately. Application metrics, then
      infrastructure metrics, then the metrics of the underlying compute
      and storage each add diagnostic detail. Each layer down fires more
      often and means less on its own — a busy processor does not
      comprise a problem unless something above it slows down. Alert at
      the top of the hierarchy by default, and keep the lower layers on
      dashboards for diagnosis. Alert low in the stack only where a hard
      limit is real, such as a disk that must not fill.
Monitoring metrics pyramid from application down to compute and storage
Each alert needs an owner and an escalation path for when the
      first responder cannot resolve it. Link each alert to a current
      runbook or playbook so any operator can respond the same way,
      keeping handling consistent across shifts. Recurring incidents
      point at a problem worth removing (for more detail, see
OPS07-BP01 Perform post-incident analysis
).
You can automate the first minutes after an alert. Configure an
      alarm to start a
CloudWatch investigation
when it fires; the investigation correlates
      related telemetry and recent changes into a probable-cause
      hypothesis before the responder arrives.
AWS DevOps Agent
can be triggered from a ticket, a webhook, or
      its own monitoring, and it then investigates autonomously and
      returns root cause analyses and mitigation plans to the channel
      that raised the alert. The alert's named owner remains accountable
      for the response.
Provider-side service events and planned lifecycle changes — such
      as a required version upgrade before automatic enforcement — can
      affect availability even when your code is unchanged. Track these
      events through an authoritative health signal, and route them into
      the same response process as internal alerts.
Implementation steps
Alert on the objectives users
            feel:
Where Application Signals tracks your
service level objectives
, create alarms on error budget burn
            rate over more than one look-back window: a short window
            that catches a fast burn and interrupts the on-call, and a
            long window that surfaces a slow steady burn as a work item.
            A burn-rate alert is actionable by construction, because it
            fires only when the objective is at risk.
Let alarms learn what normal looks
            like:
Create
anomaly detection alarms
for metrics whose normal shifts with
            traffic, so the alarm follows the learned band. Anomalies in
            trace data alert through
X-Ray insights notifications
. Keep static thresholds for
            limits that do not move, and revisit both as the workload
            changes.
Reduce noise with composite
            alarms:
Group related alarms into
composite alarms
in Amazon CloudWatch so that a single root
            cause produces one meaningful alert rather than many. Base
            each composite condition on the failure it represents, not
            on individual metrics. For OpenTelemetry workloads monitored
            in CloudWatch Omni, an
Omni alert
tracks each service as a contributor when it
            receives one result per service. As a result, one alert
            covers the fleet, and the alert's detail view identifies the
            services that are breaching.
Track provider-side events with AWS Health:
Use
AWS Health
as the authoritative source for service events
            and upcoming changes that can affect your resources.
Route
purpose-fit Health notifications
to email and chat channels,
                and integrate programmatically
through Amazon EventBridge
.
Track events that need action in the change management
                or ITSM tools you already use, such as
Jira
or
ServiceNow
.
If you use AWS Organizations, enable organizational view
                to
aggregate Health events across accounts
.
Create work items automatically from
            alarms:
Configure CloudWatch alarms to
create OpsItems in AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter
so that a
            threshold breach starts a tracked response without manual
            handoff. If your organization runs incidents in the tooling
            from step 7, route the alarm there instead. The principle is
            that no alert lands without a work item.
Create work items from events with
            EventBridge:
Create EventBridge rules that open OpsItems
for operational
            events that need action but arrive without an alarm.
Route alerts into the tools your
            organization already uses:
Send
alarm notifications
to your paging tools, such as
Opsgenie
and
PagerDuty
,
            track the response in the incident management tooling your
            teams already work in, such as
ServiceNow
or
Jira Service Management
, and relay alerts into
chat channels
where teams live in Slack or Microsoft
            Teams. An alert that arrives in an unmonitored tool is not
            actionable, however good its condition.
Hand the first minutes to
            assistants:
Configure alarms to
create investigations
, so CloudWatch investigations
            correlates related telemetry and recent changes into a
            hypothesis of the probable cause while responders are still
            being notified. Use
AWS DevOps Agent
for autonomous incident response:
            triggered from your ticketing system, a webhook, or its own
            proactive monitoring, it investigates and returns root cause
            analyses and mitigation plans to the originating ticket.
            Once your Omni space is connected to DevOps Agent, you can
            start the investigation yourself from a firing Omni alert,
            which arrives seeded with the alert's context. Assistants
            complement the response plans in these steps, while the
            owner named in each alert is accountable for the response.
Compose the full path for new
            incidents:
A single alarm can do all of the first
            minute's work:
notify
the on-call, open the incident ticket, and
start an investigation
in the same action. An
EventBridge rule
matching the investigation's status changes then
            writes its findings into the ticket as they arrive, so the
            person that picks up the ticket finds a root cause
            hypothesis within. This is how AWS and Amazon run their own
            operations, and every part of it is available to your
            workload.
Document a response plan for each
            alert type:
For each class of alert, record the
            owner, the escalation path, and the expected actions
            alongside the runbooks and playbooks that
OPS05-BP01 Develop and test runbooks to perform procedures
develops.
            Escalation paths themselves are the practice of
OPS06-BP03 Define escalation paths
.
Attach automation runbooks to the
            response:
Associate
Systems Manager Automation runbooks
with your work items so
            that
common remediation runs
as soon as one opens.
